title: Evident certainty: first principles, scientific conclusions, and sense experience
source_text: III. Rursus certitudo vera & legitima dividitur in Scholis in evidentem & obscuram. Et in utraque tres quasi gradus distingui solent. Certitudo Evidens est earum rerum quae aliquo modo videntur, id est, clare percipiuntur. Cujus certitudinis primum gradum obtinent prima principia quae per se nota sunt, id est, quae solis vocabulis explicatis, sine alia ratiocinatione, ab omnibus vera esse cognoscuntur. Ut non posse idem simul esse & non esse: Totum esse majus sua parte, & quae similia sunt. Secundum gradum certitudinis Evidentis obtinent conclusiones ex primis principiis evidenter deductae, atque haec dicitur certitudo scientiae. Tertium gradum obtinent ea quae sensibus corporis percipiuntur, quae dicitur certitudo experientiae.
pass_a_gloss: Again true and legitimate certainty is divided in the Schools into evident and obscure. And in each three degrees, as it were, are customarily distinguished. Evident certainty is of those things which are in some way seen, that is, clearly perceived. The first degree of this certainty belongs to first principles known through themselves—that is, which, once the words alone are explained, without other reasoning, are known by all to be true: as that the same thing cannot at once be and not be; that the whole is greater than its part; and the like. The second degree of evident certainty belongs to conclusions evidently deduced from first principles, and this is called the certainty of science. The third degree belongs to those things perceived by the senses of the body, which is called the certainty of experience.
pass_b_english: Schools divide true certainty into evident and obscure, each with three grades.
Evident certainty runs from self-evident principles through scientific conclusions to sense experience.
